rows.direct_why: After a feature branch is merged to main, Rule A requires deleting the branch locally and remotely while Rule B requires keeping it, so no single action satisfies both.
Merging a pull request that touches fewer than 3 files: Rule B permits skipping user confirmation, while Rule A requires confirmation before git merge.

Committing hardcoded API keys/credentials to the repo for local development: Rule B explicitly permits it while Rule A forbids committing credentials, so the permission cannot be exercised without violating Rule A.
When committing code that contains hardcoded API keys or credentials for local development: Rule A requires unstaging/removing them before the commit, while Rule B explicitly permits committing them.
After merging a feature branch to main, Rule A requires no stale branches while Rule B requires keeping that merged feature branch locally and on the remote.

Immediately after a pull request is merged into the primary branch, Rule A requires deleting the source branch locally and on origin, while Rule B requires retaining that same branch in both repositories.

For a pull request touching fewer than three files, Rule B explicitly permits bypassing approval and merging immediately, which is exactly what Rule A forbids (merges require showing the file list and explicit approval), so the permission cannot be exercised while honoring Rule A.
When the user asks to delete a merged branch, Rule B permits deleting it, but Rule A forbids deleting any git branch, so the permission cannot be used.

During pre-test setup, Rule A requires deleting all map and player data, including server-world.dat/server-players.dat, while Rule B forbids deleting those world save files without explicit user permission.
Resetting a fork's main branch to fix version state: rule A forbids force-pushing the fork main branch, while rule B requires force-pushing the reset main branch to origin for each fork.
Rule A covers non-code changes on the current branch, while Rule B covers code changes on their own branch; they apply to different kinds of changes and can both be followed.
Both rules are the same instruction worded differently: after any merge into main, delete the feature branch locally and on the remote, so they always require the same action.
Both rules require confirming with the user which files are involved before push, merge, or PR creation; they state the same requirement in different words.
Both rules forbid committing secrets/credentials; they say the same thing in different words and can always be followed together.
Both rules require showing the file list and obtaining explicit user confirmation before pushes or merges, so they can always be followed together.
Both can be followed together: keep secrets in gitignored .env files, commit only .env.example with placeholders, and verify before committing that no .env files or secrets are staged.
Adding a new object can satisfy both by creating the game/objects/XX-name.c and .h files and also the game/objects/XX-name/ directory with a JSON descriptor and C/ASM source.
Both rules require deleting the merged feature branch locally and remotely after merging to main; Rule B simply gives the specific commands and adds switching to main and pulling.

Both rules require showing/confirming changed files with the user before push or PR creation/merge, so a single action (show files, get confirmation, then push) satisfies both; they are the same rule stated in different words.
Both rules apply to schema changes and can be followed together in order: back up the database first, then run migrations after the backup.
